summary: Describes the changes to OSPF needed to support IPv6, producing what is commonly called OSPF version 3. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level, and it was replaced by RFC 5340.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF is how routers share road maps. This updates that sharing for the newer, longer IPv6 addresses.

questions: how does ospf work with ipv6
how is ospfv3 different from ospfv2
what is a link lsa in ospf
subtitle: How OSPF was adapted to route IPv6: same core machinery, with addresses moved out of the packets and into new LSAs.

tldr.problem: OSPF for IPv4 builds addresses and IPv4-specific assumptions into its packets and advertisements, so it cannot route IPv6 as it stands.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF version 3 keeps flooding, Designated Router election, areas and the shortest path calculation, but removes addressing from packet headers and the basic LSAs, runs per link, adds new LSA types for IPv6 prefixes, and relies on IPv6 security headers instead of its own authentication.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2740 was a Proposed Standard and has been replaced by RFC 5340, which is the current OSPF for IPv6 specification.

today: RFC 2740 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 5340, which is the current specification of OSPF for IPv6.

sections.title: What Changes and What Stays
sections.content:
RFC 2740 describes the changes to OSPF needed to support IPv6. The fundamental mechanisms (flooding, Designated Router election, area support, SPF calculations) remain unchanged. Changes were made either because the protocol semantics differ between IPv4 and IPv6, or simply to handle the bigger address size.

The RFC is written as a delta against OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328). The five packet types (Hello, Database Description, Link State Request, Link State Update and Link State Acknowledgment), neighbor discovery, adjacency selection, the interface and neighbor state machines, the link types and LSA aging all work as before. Optional capabilities such as on-demand circuits, NSSA areas and the multicast extensions (MOSPF) are also supported.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like updating a board game for new pieces. The rules for how players take turns stay the same, but a few cards are redrawn so the new pieces fit.

sections.title: Links, Not Subnets
sections.content:
IPv6 talks about a link rather than a subnet. Several prefixes can sit on one link, and two nodes can talk directly on a link even without a common prefix. So OSPF for IPv6 runs per link instead of per IP subnet, and an OSPF interface connects to a link.

Addressing semantics are removed from OSPF packets and from the Router-LSA and Network-LSA, which now only express topology. Router IDs, Area IDs and LSA Link State IDs stay 32 bits long and can no longer be assigned as IPv6 addresses. Neighbors are always identified by Router ID, and the Router ID 0.0.0.0 is reserved.

Packets are sent from the interface's link-local address, except on virtual links, which must use a global or site-local address. A router learns the link-local addresses of its neighbors and uses them as next hops. Link-local addresses must not be advertised in Inter-Area-Prefix-LSAs, AS-external-LSAs or Intra-Area-Prefix-LSAs.

Multiple OSPF instances can now run on one link, separated by an Instance ID in the packet header. Packets whose Instance ID differs from the receiving interface's are discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of identifying each neighbor by a house number, routers now know each other by a name tag they carry. The map itself only shows how the roads connect, and the street numbers are written on a separate page.

sections.title: The OSPF Packet Header and Options
sections.content:
OSPF for IPv6 runs directly over IPv6. The version number goes from 2 to 3, and every packet starts with a standard 16 byte header with Version, Type, Packet length, Router ID, Area ID, Checksum and Instance ID. The Authentication and AuType fields are gone. The Hello packet now contains no address information at all and carries an Interface ID that the originating router assigned to its interface to the link.

The Options field in Hello and Database Description packets grows to 24 bits. Two bits are added: the R-bit (is the originator an active router) and the V6-bit (if clear, the router or link is excluded from IPv6 routing calculations). The existing DC, N, MC and E bits remain.

The checksum is the standard IPv6 one: the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the packet, with a prepended pseudo-header whose Next Header value is 89.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a small label saying who sent it and which neighborhood it is for. The label no longer has a street address on it, so the same label design would work for any kind of address.

sections.title: LSA Types and Flooding Scope
sections.content:
The flooding scope of an LSA is now coded in its LS type field, with three values: link-local (flooded only on the local link), area (flooded through one OSPF area) and AS (flooded throughout the routing domain). A U-bit in the same field says what a router does with a type it does not recognize: treat it as link-local, or store and flood it as if understood. Silently discarding unknown types, as OSPF for IPv4 does, is unsupported because it causes problems when the Designated Router supports fewer options than other routers on the link.

Type-3 and Type-4 summary-LSAs are renamed Inter-Area-Prefix-LSAs and Inter-Area-Router-LSAs. Two LSAs are new. The Link-LSA gives a router's link-local address and its prefixes on a link to the other routers there. The Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA carries the IPv6 prefix information that IPv4 put in Router-LSAs and Network-LSAs. For Network-LSAs and Link-LSAs the Link State ID is the originator's Interface ID.

AS-external-LSAs may now omit the forwarding address and the external route tag, and can reference another LSA to carry extra route attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Some notes are only for people on your street, some are for your whole neighborhood, and some are for the whole town. The note itself now says which group should get it.

sections.title: Stub Areas and Unknown LSAs
sections.content:
Stub areas are kept to shrink link-state databases for routers with few resources. Among the mandatory types, stub areas carry only Router-LSAs, Network-LSAs, Inter-Area-Prefix-LSAs, Link-LSAs and Intra-Area-Prefix-LSAs.

Because unknown LSAs can be flooded, an uncontrolled flood could overload a stub area. The rule is that an LSA of unrecognized type may be flooded into or through a stub area only if it has area or link-local scope and its U-bit is 0.
sections.plainLanguage: A small village does not need the full town map. So only the simple kinds of notes are allowed in, so the village's little notice board does not overflow.

sections.title: Authentication Moves to IPv6
sections.content:
Authentication is removed from OSPF itself. The AuType and Authentication fields are gone from the header and from the area and interface structures. Running over IPv6, OSPF relies on the IP Authentication Header and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload for integrity and authentication or confidentiality of routing exchanges. Protection against accidental corruption comes from the standard IPv6 checksum.

When IPsec protects OSPF packets, an implementation must check the IPsec security association and the local SA database to make sure the packet comes from a source trusted for OSPF purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every OSPF message carrying its own secret handshake, routers use the lock that IPv6 already provides for all traffic.

fields.name: Version #
fields.desc: OSPF version number; this specification documents version 3.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Packet type, 1 to 5: Hello, Database Description, Link State Request, Link State Update, Link State Acknowledgment.

fields.name: Packet length
fields.desc: Length of the OSPF packet in bytes, including this header.

fields.name: Router ID
fields.desc: Router ID of the packet's source.

fields.name: Area ID
fields.desc: 32-bit number identifying the area the packet belongs to.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Standard IPv6 checksum with a pseudo-header; Next Header value 89.

fields.name: Instance ID
fields.desc: Lets multiple OSPF instances run over one link.

items.label: Router-LSA
items.desc: Area scope; state and cost of a router's interfaces to the area.

items.label: Network-LSA
items.desc: Area scope; lists the routers on a link.

items.label: AS-External-LSA
items.desc: AS scope; routes outside the routing domain.

items.label: Link-LSA
items.desc: Link-local scope; new in OSPF for IPv6.

items.label: Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA
items.desc: Area scope; new, carries IPv6 prefix information.
